scenarios.evidence: measured against similar stops without reform
scenarios.info: From our own lot-by-lot data on 16 US places that upzoned land near rail or rapid transit. For each, we compared building near the reform's stations with building near similar stations without a reform, before and after. A model trained on these places, tested by hiding one place at a time, beat simple rules only within a quarter mile of stops. Places that upzoned a small area near their stations gained; places that upzoned most of the land near every station (Los Angeles, San Diego, Chicago in 2022, Honolulu) gained about nothing so far. Wisconsin's law is broad, so the model puts it with them: about 40 extra homes over five years, between about −160 and 340 — about the same as no reform. If the broad programs' affordable-housing requirements are what held them back, it would be about 210. Caution: near Milwaukee's new streetcar, building rose by a similar amount with no rezoning at all. This replaced the earlier little line, Los Angeles's Transit Oriented Communities program (171), shown as a comparison.
scenarios.label: Little or no response
scenarios.source: Station-area lot model: 43.1 extra homes over 2027-2031 (range -161.0 to 342.8), reference/tod_station_area_line.csv; New York pooled ramp

scenarios.info: From our own lot-by-lot data on 16 US places that upzoned land near rail or rapid transit, compared with similar stations without reform. Averaged over the places, building within a quarter mile of reform stations rose by about 69 extra homes per 100 acres a year for each part of the land upzoned (the rule set in advance: one pooled ratio, each place counted once). Wisconsin's law would upzone about 71% of the land within a quarter mile of rail and rapid stops, giving about 13,200 extra homes over 2027–2031 (range about 9,100 to 17,100, leaving out one place at a time). Treat it as what Wisconsin could get if it did as well as the average reform city. Across the places, the measured effect fell, not rose, with coverage (rank correlation −0.66 within a quarter mile): a line fitted through them at Wisconsin's 71% gives about −570, and the five broad places alone about −460, while the plain average without scaling gives about 5,950. Near Milwaukee's new streetcar building also rose by a similar amount without any rezoning. So this is closer to an upper estimate; its range shows only the effect of leaving out one place at a time, not this disagreement. The earlier central line (the upzoned-share trend in 9 cities, 1,196) is shown as a comparison.
scenarios.label: Central: if Wisconsin did as well as the average reform city
scenarios.source: Average reform city at Wisconsin's coverage: 13,229 extra homes over 2027-2031 (range 9,147-17,108), reference/tod_station_area_line.csv; New York pooled ramp

scenarios.info: Like Auckland, New Zealand, which upzoned three-quarters of its residential land in 2016 and permitted 21,808 extra homes over 2016–2021, net of building moved from elsewhere in the city.
scenarios.label: Strong response
scenarios.source: Auckland: 21,808 / 530,300 = 4.11% / 0.752 coverage; Auckland 2017-2021 profile rescaled to the stated total

timing_caveat: The studies measured their effects three or more years after each reform. The model places that effect inside 2027–2031, the law's first five years. Much of a real law's effect may come after 2031, so the yearly path is the least certain part of these numbers.
